EnerGNN: Learning Optimization-Compatible Energy Functions for Exact Constrained Combinatorial Inference

Niki Triantafyllou ††thanks: Corresponding author.    Maria M. Papathanasiou Affiliation: Sargent Centre for Process Systems Engineering, Department of Chemical Engineering Affiliation: Imperial College London Email: {niki.triantafyllou20,maria.papathanasiou11}@imperial.ac.uk
Abstract

Learning-based approaches to combinatorial optimization often predict solutions directly or use predictions to restrict search, while expressive energy-based models typically rely on approximate inference. We introduce EnerGNN, a framework that learns energy functions over complete binary configurations and minimizes them under explicit hard constraints through mixed integer programming (MIP). EnerGNN combines a graph neural network encoder with an optimization-compatible readout and a nonlinear energy head, enabling exact constrained inference over the learned energy. An optimality-aware contrastive loss trains the energy to reflect solution quality and constraint violations. Across Quadratic Knapsack, Combinatorial Auctions, and a personalized cell therapy supply chain problem, EnerGNN achieves near-optimal solutions with 100% feasibility. On the supply chain problem, it achieves a 0.05% mean primal gap and a 17.4×\times speedup over the monolithic MIP. The learned energy also generalizes to larger instances and supports zero-shot constraint injection, adapting to changing constraints without retraining while preserving feasibility.

1 Introduction

A central challenge in energy-based structured prediction is to combine expressive learned representations with tractable inference over structured outputs. Energy-based models (EBMs) assign scalar energies to complete output configurations, allowing dependencies and interactions between output variables to be captured through learned energy functions (LeCun et al., 2006; Belanger and McCallum, 2016). However, minimizing expressive neural energies over discrete decision spaces is generally challenging, particularly when solutions must satisfy hard operational, physical, or logical constraints. Mixed integer programming (MIP) provides a framework for enforcing such constraints and obtaining globally optimal solutions, but learned energy functions must admit suitable mathematical representations to be optimized directly. This creates an interface problem between neural learning and exact optimization: How can a neural model learn expressive energy functions that an exact optimizer can minimize under hard constraints?

Existing approaches address different aspects of this challenge. In learning-based combinatorial optimization, neural models have been used to construct solutions, predict variable assignments, and guide exact solvers (Bengio et al., 2021; Khalil et al., 2017; Gasse et al., 2019). Methods such as Neural Diving (Nair et al., 2020) and ConPaS (Huang et al., 2024) use learned variable-level predictions to identify promising regions of the solution space, which are then explored through restricted optimization. In energy-based structured prediction, inference with expressive neural energies commonly relies on continuous relaxations, gradient-based optimization, or approximate decoding (Belanger and McCallum, 2016; Graber and Schwing, 2019). Meanwhile, ReLU neural networks can be represented exactly using mixed integer formulations (Fischetti and Jo, 2018; Anderson et al., 2020), providing a mechanism for optimizing learned nonlinear functions under explicit constraints. Together, these developments motivate learning energy functions that are designed to be directly optimized under explicit hard constraints, bringing expressive structured prediction and exact combinatorial inference into a unified framework.

We introduce EnerGNN, an energy-based framework that learns optimization-compatible energy functions over complete binary configurations and minimizes them subject to explicit hard constraints. As illustrated in Figure 1, EnerGNN combines a bipartite message-passing graph neural network (GNN) encoder with a decision-dependent readout and a piecewise linear ReLU energy head. The GNN encoder produces representations of the problem instance that are computed once and remain fixed during optimization. The readout combines these fixed representations with the binary decision variables to construct a configuration-dependent representation. Together, the readout and nonlinear ReLU energy head allow EnerGNN to model interactions between decision variables while admitting an exact MIP representation. At inference, the learned energy is minimized over the full encoded feasible region using a MIP solver, yielding a feasible solution that is globally optimal with respect to the learned energy when solved to optimality.

A key feature of EnerGNN is the separation of learned preferences from explicit feasibility constraints. The energy-based model learns to distinguish high-quality configurations from suboptimal alternatives through optimality-aware contrastive training, while hard constraints are enforced directly during inference. This separation allows the same learned energy to be optimized under different feasible regions, without retraining the model. In particular, deployment-time constraints can be added, removed, or modified by changing the inference MIP, enabling zero-shot constraint injection. This approach is complementary to neural algorithmic reasoning (Veličković and Blundell, 2021): rather than learning to execute an optimization algorithm, EnerGNN learns an energy function over structured decisions and delegates constrained inference to an exact optimizer.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate constrained combinatorial inference as learning an optimization-compatible energy over complete binary configurations, separating learned preferences from explicit hard constraints. Second, we develop a graph-based energy architecture that captures nonlinear interactions between decision variables while admitting exact MIP representation and globally optimal inference with respect to the learned energy. Third, we develop an optimality-aware contrastive learning objective using feasible and infeasible candidate configurations to learn solution-level energy landscapes. We evaluate EnerGNN on Quadratic Knapsack (QKP), Combinatorial Auctions (CA), and a personalized cell therapy supply chain problem (CART). Our experiments demonstrate the benefits of nonlinear energy modeling for interaction-heavy objectives, the ability to obtain near-optimal solutions while satisfying hard constraints, generalization to larger problem sizes, and zero-shot constraint injection without retraining. The code and data used in this work are available at https://github.com/nikitrian/EnerGNN.

2 Related Work

Learning-based methods for combinatorial optimization. Learning-based approaches to combinatorial optimization commonly use neural models to amortize expensive search across related problem instances. Neural combinatorial optimization methods learn policies that construct solutions sequentially using graph-based or attention-based architectures, often trained through reinforcement learning (Khalil et al., 2017; Bello et al., 2016; Kool et al., 2019; Kwon et al., 2020). Another line of work integrates learning into branch-and-bound algorithms, including branching-variable selection (Khalil et al., 2016; Gasse et al., 2019; Gupta et al., 2020) and search-tree node selection (He et al., 2014). Learning-based predict-and-search methods instead use neural predictions to identify promising variable assignments and solve reduced or restricted optimization problems. Neural Diving predicts distributions over variable assignments and fixes subsets of variables before solving reduced subproblems (Nair et al., 2020). Predict-and-Search (PaS) uses GNN predictions to define search neighborhoods around predicted solutions (Han et al., 2023), while Contrastive Predict-and-Search (ConPaS) extends this approach with contrastive learning to improve solution prediction (Huang et al., 2024).

Differentiable optimization and constraint enforcement. Decision-focused learning trains predictive models using downstream decision quality, while differentiable optimization methods integrate optimization problems into neural networks and propagate learning signals through their solutions (Amos and Kolter, 2017; Agrawal et al., 2019; Ferber et al., 2020; Paulus et al., 2021; Parmentier, 2025). These approaches enable learning of optimization problem parameters, including objective coefficients and, in some formulations, constraints. Related methods enforce feasibility of neural predictions through differentiable correction, projection, or constraint-enforcement layers (Donti et al., 2021; Min and Azizan, 2024; Wang et al., 2023; Tordesillas et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2024). Unlike differentiable optimization approaches, EnerGNN uses the MIP solver for inference without differentiating through it during training.

Energy-based structured prediction. Structured Prediction Energy Networks (SPENs) learn expressive energy functions over structured outputs and perform inference through continuous relaxation and gradient-based optimization (Belanger and McCallum, 2016). Input Convex Neural Networks (ICNNs) impose convexity with respect to the optimized inputs, enabling globally optimal inference in continuous convex settings (Amos et al., 2017). Graph Structured Prediction Energy Networks combine explicit local structure with learned higher-order interactions and perform iterative inference over a constrained relaxation (Graber and Schwing, 2019). Blondel et al. (2022) develop generalized Fenchel–Young losses for training energy networks without differentiating through the inference optimization problem. Energy-based models have also been integrated into decision-focused stochastic optimization, where learned energy functions are used to approximate optimization landscapes (Kong et al., 2022). More recently, Huang et al. (2026) propose an energy-based Langevin sampler for mixed integer optimization, combining neural sampling of integer variables with linear programming for continuous variables. EnerGNN builds on energy-based structured prediction but designs its learned energy function to admit an exact MIP representation, enabling global minimization over binary configurations under explicit hard constraints without requiring convexity.

Mixed integer representations of neural networks. Piecewise linear neural networks, particularly ReLU networks, can be represented exactly using mixed integer linear constraints (Tjeng et al., 2017; Fischetti and Jo, 2018; Anderson et al., 2020; Tsay et al., 2021). These formulations have been used for neural network verification and for embedding trained neural surrogate models inside optimization problems. Bound-tightening techniques can improve the strength and computational performance of these formulations (Grimstad and Andersson, 2019). EnerGNN uses these formulations to optimize a learned energy over binary configurations, with the GNN encoder evaluated before optimization and the readout and ReLU energy head represented exactly within the MIP formulation.

3 Methodology

We present the EnerGNN framework, which combines energy learning over binary configurations with exact constrained inference through mixed integer optimization. We first formulate the learning and inference problems, then describe the graph-based energy architecture, the training objective, and its exact MIP encoding. Finally, we establish the theoretical properties of the resulting framework.

3.1 Problem Setting

We consider mixed integer optimization problems of the form

min𝐲,𝐱\displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x}} f⁡(𝐲,𝐱)\displaystyle f(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x}) (1)
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} 𝐀𝐲+𝐁𝐱≤𝐛,\displaystyle\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{B}\mathbf{x}\leq\mathbf{b},
𝐲∈{0,1}n.\displaystyle\mathbf{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n}.

where yy denotes binary decision variables and xx denotes any remaining operational variables.

We consider two settings. In direct decision problems, such as Quadratic Knapsack (QKP) and Combinatorial Auctions (CA), 𝐲\mathbf{y} constitutes the full decision vector. In hierarchical decomposition problems, such as the cell therapy supply chain problem (CART), 𝐲\mathbf{y} represents high-level planning decisions whose assignments define a reduced downstream scheduling problem. In the latter setting, fixing 𝐲\mathbf{y} induces the value function

F⁡(𝐲)=min𝐱⁡{f⁡(𝐲,𝐱)|𝐀𝐲+𝐁𝐱≤𝐛}.F(\mathbf{y})=\min_{\mathbf{x}}\left\{f(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x})\;\middle|\;\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{B}\mathbf{x}\leq\mathbf{b}\right\}. (2)

EnerGNN does not attempt to reproduce the original objective analytically. Instead, it learns an energy function Eθ​(𝒢,𝐲)E_{\theta}(\mathcal{G},\mathbf{y}) over assignments of the binary decision variables, referred to as configurations, where 𝒢\mathcal{G} is a graph representation of the problem instance. Training uses solver-generated candidate configurations and their associated solution quality to learn an ordering in which lower energies correspond to higher-quality configurations. For direct decision problems, this ordering reflects the original objective, while for hierarchical decision problems it approximates the ordering induced by F⁡(𝐲)F(\mathbf{y}).

At inference, the learned energy is minimized subject to explicit hard constraints:

𝐲⋆∈arg⁡min𝐲∈{0,1}n\displaystyle\mathbf{y}^{\star}\in\arg\min_{\mathbf{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n}} Eθ​(𝒢,𝐲)\displaystyle E_{\theta}(\mathcal{G},\mathbf{y}) (3)
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} 𝐀y​𝐲≤𝐛y.\displaystyle\mathbf{A}_{y}\mathbf{y}\leq\mathbf{b}_{y}.

The constraints define the feasible set, while the learned energy defines the objective optimized over that set. This formulation defines Neural-MIP inference.

3.2 Architecture Design

Graph Neural Network Encoder.

Each instance is represented as a bipartite graph 𝒢=(𝒞∪𝒱,ℰ)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{C}\cup\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}), where 𝒱\mathcal{V} denotes the binary decision variables and 𝒞\mathcal{C} represents constraints or interactions, depending on the problem structure. Following the variable-constraint graph representation commonly used for learning in MIP solvers (Gasse et al., 2019), a bipartite message-passing GNN produces node embeddings {𝐡v}v∈𝒱\{\mathbf{h}_{v}\}_{v\in\mathcal{V}} and {𝐡c}c∈𝒞\{\mathbf{h}_{c}\}_{c\in\mathcal{C}}, together with a global graph embedding 𝐡𝒢\mathbf{h}_{\mathcal{G}}. The encoder is evaluated once per instance, and its outputs remain fixed during optimization.

Optimization-Compatible Readout.

To enable exact optimization, the mapping 𝐲↦𝐳0\mathbf{y}\mapsto\mathbf{z}^{0} must admit a mixed integer linear representation. We construct a benchmark-specific readout that combines the embeddings of selected binary variables with additional structural features:

𝐳0​(𝐲)=[∑v∈𝒱yv​𝐡v,𝐳lin​(𝐲),𝐡𝒢].\mathbf{z}^{0}(\mathbf{y})=\Bigl[\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}y_{v}\mathbf{h}_{v},\;\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{lin}}(\mathbf{y}),\;\mathbf{h}_{\mathcal{G}}\Bigr]. (4)

The additional features 𝐳lin​(𝐲)\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{lin}}(\mathbf{y}) capture problem-specific information, such as unselected-item embeddings and capacity utilization in QKP, or occupied-item embeddings in CA. The global graph embedding 𝐡𝒢\mathbf{h}_{\mathcal{G}} provides an instance-level representation that remains fixed across binary configurations. All decision-dependent readout components are either affine in 𝐲\mathbf{y} or admit exact linearization using auxiliary variables. Benchmark-specific graph representations and readout definitions are provided in Appendix B.

Energy Head.

A multilayer perceptron (MLP) with ReLU activations maps 𝐳0​(𝐲)\mathbf{z}^{0}(\mathbf{y}) to a scalar energy Eθ​(𝒢,𝐲)E_{\theta}(\mathcal{G},\mathbf{y}). The nonlinear energy head enables the model to capture interactions between binary decisions, while its piecewise linear structure, combined with the optimization-compatible readout, admits an exact mixed integer linear representation.

3.3 Optimality-Aware Energy Learning

We train on candidate configurations 𝒴=ℱ∪ℐ\mathcal{Y}=\mathcal{F}\cup\mathcal{I}, containing feasible and infeasible configurations. Each feasible candidate 𝐲i\mathbf{y}_{i} is assigned a relative primal gap gig_{i}, measured against the best available reference solution for that instance, while each infeasible candidate 𝐲k\mathbf{y}_{k} is associated with a normalized constraint violation magnitude νk\nu_{k}. The loss combines an optimality-aware contrastive term, feasible calibration, and infeasibility shaping:

ℒ=ℒcon+λcal​ℒcal+λinf​ℒinf.\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{con}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{cal}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cal}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{inf}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{inf}}. (5)

Optimality-aware contrastive loss.

For each instance, we construct a target distribution that assigns greater probability to feasible configurations with smaller primal gaps and zero probability to infeasible configurations. The learned energy induces a second distribution over the entire candidate pool, and the Kullback–Leibler divergence encourages the two distributions to agree.

ℒcon\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{con}} =KL(p⋆∥pθ),\displaystyle=\mathrm{KL}(p^{\star}\,\|\,p_{\theta}), (6)
pi∗\displaystyle p_{i}^{*} ={exp(−gi/τrank)∑j∈ℱexp(−gj/τrank),i∈ℱ,0,i∉ℱ,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\exp(-g_{i}/\tau_{\mathrm{rank}})}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{F}}\exp(-g_{j}/\tau_{\mathrm{rank}})},&i\in\mathcal{F},\\[8.00003pt] 0,&i\notin\mathcal{F},\end{cases}
pθ,i\displaystyle p_{\theta,i} =exp(−Eθ(𝒢,𝐲i)/T)∑j∈𝒴exp(−Eθ(𝒢,𝐲j)/T),i∈𝒴.\displaystyle=\dfrac{\exp(-E_{\theta}(\mathcal{G},\mathbf{y}_{i})/T)}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{Y}}\exp(-E_{\theta}(\mathcal{G},\mathbf{y}_{j})/T)},\qquad i\in\mathcal{Y}.

where TT is the model softmax temperature and τrank\tau_{\mathrm{rank}} controls the target sharpness.

Calibration loss.

The contrastive loss primarily supervises relative preferences within the candidate pool. We additionally calibrate the energies of feasible configurations against their relative primal gaps using Huber regression with an instance-adaptive transition scale.

ℒcal=1|ℱ|​∑i∈ℱHδℱ​(Eθ​(𝒢,𝐲i)−gi).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cal}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{F}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{F}}H_{\delta_{\mathcal{F}}}\!\left(E_{\theta}(\mathcal{G},\mathbf{y}_{i})-g_{i}\right). (7)

The transition scale δℱ\delta_{\mathcal{F}} is computed from the primal-gap span of feasible candidates. Details are given in Appendix E.

Infeasibility loss.

For infeasible configurations, we use an auxiliary Huber loss to align their energies with a logarithmically scaled measure of constraint violation:

ℒinf=1|ℐ|​∑k∈ℐHδinf​(Eθ​(𝒢,𝐲k)−log⁡(1+νk)),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{inf}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}|}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}}H_{\delta_{\mathrm{inf}}}\!\left(E_{\theta}(\mathcal{G},\mathbf{y}_{k})-\log(1+\nu_{k})\right), (8)

where νk≥0\nu_{k}\geq 0 is the normalized constraint violation. This term provides a graded training signal within the infeasible region, while ℒcon\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{con}} discourages infeasible candidates from receiving probability mass at the expense of high-quality feasible configurations. Feasibility at inference is enforced explicitly by the MIP constraints.

3.4 Inference via Neural-MIP Encoding

At inference, the trained GNN encoder is evaluated once, while the decision-dependent readout and ReLU energy head are represented exactly within the MIP using auxiliary variables and linear constraints. Valid pre-activation bounds are obtained through interval bound propagation using benchmark-specific input bounds (Gowal et al., 2018). Neurons with fixed activation states are eliminated to reduce the formulation size. The exact Neural-MIP formulation is detailed in Appendix C, with the bound-tightening procedure described in Appendix C.2.

3.5 Theoretical Properties

We summarize the formal properties induced by the architectural design. Detailed proofs are provided in Appendix A.

Proposition 3.1 (MIP-representable energy).

For a fixed instance graph 𝒢\mathcal{G}, assume that the encoder is evaluated once, the readout 𝐳0​(𝐲)\mathbf{z}^{0}(\mathbf{y}) admits an exact mixed integer linear representation over a bounded domain, and the energy head is a feed-forward ReLU network. Then 𝐲↦Eθ​(𝒢,𝐲)\mathbf{y}\mapsto E_{\theta}(\mathcal{G},\mathbf{y}) is exactly MIP-representable on that domain.

Proof sketch.

For fixed 𝒢\mathcal{G}, encoder outputs are constants. The readout admits an exact mixed integer linear representation by construction. A ReLU network is a composition of affine maps and ReLU operators, each of which admits an exact mixed integer linear encoding over bounded input domains. Hence the full energy admits an exact MIP representation. ∎

Corollary 3.2 (Exact feasible inference).

If the encoded feasible set

𝒞={𝐲∈{0,1}n∣𝐀y​𝐲≤𝐛y}\mathcal{C}=\left\{\mathbf{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n}\mid\mathbf{A}_{y}\mathbf{y}\leq\mathbf{b}_{y}\right\}

is nonempty, then solving

min𝐲∈𝒞⁡Eθ​(𝒢,𝐲)\min_{\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{C}}E_{\theta}(\mathcal{G},\mathbf{y})

is equivalent to solving a mixed integer linear program and returns a feasible solution that is globally optimal with respect to the learned energy.

Corollary 3.3 (Constraint injection).

The same learned energy can be optimized over any bounded test-time feasible set obtained by adding, removing, or modifying linear constraints over the same decision variables, without retraining the EBM. If the test-time feasible set is not contained in the domain used to compute the original Big-M bounds, the bounds used in the MIP encoding must be recomputed for the new feasible set.

Proposition 3.4 (Expressivity beyond factorized scoring).

If the readout contains the binary variables 𝐲\mathbf{y}, or an affine representation from which they can be recovered, a one-hidden-layer ReLU energy can represent arbitrary quadratic pairwise interactions over binary variables exactly, whereas a factorized linear score cannot represent a nonzero pairwise interaction.

4 Experiments

We evaluate EnerGNN on three combinatorial optimization problems: Quadratic Knapsack (QKP), Combinatorial Auctions (CA), and a Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy supply chain (CART). QKP and CA evaluate direct decision inference, while CART considers hierarchical decomposition, where EnerGNN selects high-level capacitated facility location decisions before solving a reduced downstream patient scheduling problem. Our experiments assess solution quality, feasibility, the contribution of nonlinear energy modeling, cross-scale generalization, and zero-shot constraint injection. Each benchmark examines a different aspect of the framework: QKP tests nonlinear interactions between variables, CA evaluates inference under packing constraints, and CART examines learning over complicating variables in hierarchical optimization.

4.1 Benchmarks

Quadratic Knapsack. QKP is an interaction-heavy problem involving the selection of items under a capacity constraint, with both individual profits and pairwise interactions contributing to the objective. We consider instances with 150 binary item-selection variables and an interaction density of 0.30.

Cell Therapy Supply Chain. CART is a time-indexed, capacitated facility location and patient allocation MIP for personalized CAR T-cell therapy supply chains. The network comprises 16 candidate manufacturing facilities. The formulation incorporates 2 transportation modes and daily scheduling over a 130-day horizon, with patient demand varying from 10 to 650 across different demand distributions. EnerGNN optimizes the 16 first-stage facility location variables, with each configuration of these variables inducing a tactical patient scheduling MIP.

Combinatorial Auctions. CA is a packing problem with 175 binary bid-selection variables, extended to 250 in the cross-scale evaluation. Each bid consumes a subset of items, and each item can be allocated at most once. Because the original objective is linear and these instances are comparatively easy for modern MIP solvers, CA primarily evaluates constrained inference and generalization rather than computational speedup.

Detailed benchmark problem formulations are given in Appendix B. Instance generation procedures and dataset statistics are described in Appendix D. Benchmark-specific Neural-MIP input bounds and hard feasibility constraints are detailed in Appendices C.3 and C.4, respectively.

4.2 Baselines and Metrics

We compare against three classes of baselines that differ in how learning is combined with optimization. Full MIP solves the original problem using branch-and-cut and provides a reference optimum. Predict+Search, Neural Diving (Nair et al., 2020), and ConPaS (Huang et al., 2024) use learned predictions to restrict or guide the solver’s search. Predict+Search fixes variables based on prediction confidence and solves the resulting reduced problem. Neural Diving samples variable assignments, fixes subsets of variables, and solves multiple reduced subproblems. ConPaS instead imposes a neighborhood constraint around its learned prediction while retaining the original objective.

Linear+MIP and EnerGNN learn objectives that are optimized directly under explicit hard constraints. Linear+MIP uses additive per-variable scores, whereas EnerGNN learns a joint energy over complete configurations that can capture interactions between decisions. We evaluate Linear+MIP with binary cross-entropy (BCE) and contrastive supervision, and include EnerGNN (Linear) as an ablation that replaces the ReLU energy head with a linear head over the same readout. This isolates the contribution of the nonlinear energy head. All learning-based methods use the same bipartite GNN encoder and input features where applicable, but differ in their prediction heads, training objectives, and inference procedures. Full implementation details and inference settings are provided in Appendix K.

We report mean primal gap, runtime, feasibility, and the fraction of instances with a primal gap of at most 1%1\% relative to the certified global optimum. Primal gaps are computed over all test instances, assigning a 100%100\% penalty to infeasible outputs. EnerGNN achieves 100%100\% feasibility across the reported experiments, with hard constraints enforced directly during inference.

4.3 Main Results

Table 1 summarizes the results across the three benchmarks.

On QKP, EnerGNN (MLP) achieves the lowest mean primal gap among learning-based methods at 0.31%, with 99% of instances within 1% of the global optimum and 100% feasibility. ConPaS, Neural Diving, and Predict+Search achieve mean gaps of 0.95%, 1.04%, and 1.13%, respectively, while the linear scoring baselines perform substantially worse. The difference between EnerGNN (MLP) and its linear head ablation (0.31% versus 26.87%) is particularly informative. Both use the same graph encoder and decision-dependent readout, but the nonlinear head can capture additional interactions between readout features. Predict+Search, Neural Diving, and ConPaS remain faster, illustrating a trade-off between solution quality and inference time.

On CART, the strategic facility location decisions determine a much larger downstream patient allocation MIP. Neural Diving and ConPaS use learned predictions to restrict the strategic search, achieving mean gaps of 1.53% and 0.02% in 398.34 s and 3404.19 s, respectively. While Neural Diving uses parallel dives, allowing flips in the ConPaS neighborhood requires retaining all candidate facilities in our CART formulation, preventing the elimination of facility-dependent patient allocation dimensions. EnerGNN instead learns the downstream value of complete strategic configurations offline and optimizes this learned energy during inference. Once the facility configuration is selected, the operational MIP is constructed using only the selected facilities, reducing the number of variables and constraints by approximately 77% (Appendix F). EnerGNN achieves a 0.05% mean gap in 214.03 s, with all test instances within 1% of the global optimum and 100% feasibility, making it approximately 1.9×\times faster than Neural Diving, 15.9×\times faster than ConPaS, and 17.4×\times faster than the monolithic MIP.

On CA, the full MIP is solved by Gurobi in 0.14 s, so this benchmark is not intended to demonstrate solver acceleration. Instead, it tests whether a learned energy can be optimized under a large number of explicit packing constraints. The linear EnerGNN head achieves a 0.20% mean gap with 95% of instances within 1% of the optimum and 100% feasibility. It outperforms the nonlinear variant, which achieves a 0.53% mean gap at substantially higher inference cost. In contrast to QKP, CA has a linear original objective, and the linear energy head performs better on these instances. These results indicate that the benefit of nonlinear energy heads depends on the problem structure.

Figure 2 further examines whether the learned energy reflects the quality of complete configurations. The strong rank correlations between energy and primal gap across QKP, CART, and CA (ρ≥0.94\rho\geq 0.94) indicate that lower energy configurations generally correspond to better solutions.

4.4 Cross-Scale Generalization

We evaluate whether EnerGNN transfers to different problem sizes without retraining. In the CART setting, the model is trained on instances with m=16m=16 candidate facilities, and is evaluated at m=12m=12 and m=20m=20. In CA, the number of binary bid variables increases from 175 during training to 250 at test time. Table 2 shows that EnerGNN maintains 100% feasibility across all evaluated scales. In CART, the model achieves a mean gap of 0.98% when transferred to m=12m=12 facilities and 1.23% when extrapolated to m=20m=20, compared with 0.05% at the training scale. For CA, we report the linear head variant of EnerGNN, which achieves the best performance on this benchmark. Results for the nonlinear energy head are provided in Appendix I. Increasing the number of bids from 175 to 250 increases the mean primal gap from 0.20% to 0.98%. These results show that the learned energy can be applied to variable spaces of different sizes without retraining, although solution quality degrades under larger extrapolation shifts.

4.5 Zero-Shot Constraint Injection

We evaluate whether a trained EnerGNN can be reused after the feasible region changes without retraining. The learned energy is held fixed, and only the constraints of the inference MIP are modified. In CART (m=16m=16), we deactivate one, two, or three facilities selected in the original optimum. In CA, we remove 5, 10, or 15 bids selected in the original optimal allocation, corresponding to approximately 20%, 40%, and 60% of the selected bids, respectively, and additionally test a setting in which the highest-value bid rejected by the original optimal solution is forced into the allocation. The CART evaluation comprises 1,092 perturbations in total (319, 431, and 342 cases for removing one, two, and three selected facilities, respectively). For CA, each bid-removal setting is evaluated over 1,100 perturbations, while the forced-bid setting contains 100 perturbations. For CA constraint-injection experiments, we use the linear EnerGNN variant, which performs best on the in-distribution CA benchmark.

Table 3 compares EnerGNN with Neural Diving and ConPaS under the same constraint shifts. EnerGNN remains feasible in every case and achieves the lowest mean gap across all tested perturbations. On CART, its mean gap increases from 0.21% to 0.45% as one to three originally selected facilities are deactivated, while maintaining at least 91.23% of instances within 1% of the modified global optimum. By contrast, Neural Diving degrades substantially under the same shifts, reaching only 49.12% feasibility when three facilities are deactivated, while ConPaS exhibits larger gaps than EnerGNN across all CART perturbations. On CA, EnerGNN achieves mean gaps between 0.07% and 0.21%, with at least 93.36% of instances within 1% of the modified optimum. Both baselines obtain substantially larger gaps across all CA constraint shifts. The perturbations induce substantial changes in the selected solutions, with a mean Hamming shift of 6.26 when three CART facilities are deactivated and 41.36 when 15 CA bids are removed. Additional constraint-injection experiments are reported in Appendix H.

4.6 Loss Ablations

We ablate the loss components used to shape the energy landscape. The full loss combines an optimality-aware contrastive loss, feasible calibration, and infeasibility shaping. We additionally evaluate an alternative loss enforcing strict feasible–infeasible ordering in Appendix J.3. Table 4 shows that the calibration loss is important for learning an energy scale that reflects solution quality. Removing calibration increases the mean gap on CART from 0.05%0.05\% to 0.78%0.78\% and reduces the fraction of instances within 1%1\% of the global optimum from 100%100\% to 70%70\%. On QKP, the corresponding fraction decreases from 99%99\% to 68%68\%, while the largest degradation occurs on CA, where the mean gap increases from 0.53%0.53\% to 7.69%7.69\% and only 4%4\% of instances remain within 1%1\% of the optimum. In contrast, removing the infeasibility term has only a limited effect across all three benchmarks, suggesting that its contribution to solution quality is comparatively small.

4.7 Inference Size and Tractability

Table 5 reports the size of the Neural-MIP, where |𝐲||\mathbf{y}| denotes the original binary variables optimized by EnerGNN. The graph encoder is evaluated once before optimization and therefore does not contribute optimization variables. Additional binaries arise from the exact readout linearizations and the compact ReLU energy head. Appendix J.1 shows that increasing the width or depth of the energy head substantially increases inference time without improving solution quality.

4.8 Limitations

EnerGNN requires the decision-dependent energy head to remain MIP-representable, creating an expressiveness–tractability trade-off in the embedded component. In our experiments, compact shallow heads are sufficient, while increasing width or depth can substantially increase inference time without systematically improving solution quality. Additional representational capacity can instead be placed in the GNN encoder, which is evaluated before optimization and does not increase Neural-MIP size. Training also relies on solver-generated candidate configurations and labels, introducing a one-time offline cost that is most appropriate for repeated-deployment settings; a complete cost and amortization analysis is provided in Appendix D.1. Finally, exact inference is with respect to the learned energy rather than the original objective. Constraint injection guarantees feasibility with respect to the encoded constraints, but solution quality may degrade under sufficiently large distribution or feasible-set shifts.

5 Conclusion

We introduced EnerGNN, an energy-based framework that learns optimization-compatible energy functions over binary configurations and minimizes them under explicit hard constraints through mixed integer optimization. The framework combines a graph-based encoder with a MIP-representable readout and nonlinear energy head, enabling exact optimization of the learned energy.

Our experiments demonstrate the framework across direct decision and hierarchical decomposition settings. EnerGNN achieves near-optimal solutions with 100% feasibility across Quadratic Knapsack, Combinatorial Auctions, and a personalized cell therapy supply chain problem. On the latter, EnerGNN achieves substantial computational speedups over the monolithic MIP and learning-based baselines while maintaining near-optimal solution quality. EnerGNN also generalizes to larger problem instances without retraining and supports zero-shot constraint injection, allowing the same learned energy to be optimized under changing operational constraints while preserving feasibility. This adaptability is particularly valuable in deployment settings where operational requirements and resource availability may change over time.

More broadly, EnerGNN suggests a design principle for reliable AI systems. When discrete decisions must satisfy hard constraints, learning can shape objectives that algorithmic modules optimize rather than producing final decisions directly. This shifts the learned object from the decision itself to an optimization-compatible objective over decisions, allowing learned preferences and explicit constraints to remain separate at inference.

Appendix A Proofs of Theoretical Properties

We provide the proofs for the theoretical properties stated in Section 3.5. Throughout this appendix, the instance graph 𝒢\mathcal{G} is fixed. The graph encoder is evaluated once before inference, and its outputs are treated as constants. The optimization variables in Neural-MIP inference are therefore the original binary decision variables, the readout auxiliary variables, the ReLU activation variables, and the scalar energy variable.

A.1 Preliminaries

Definition A.1 (MIP-representability).

Let 𝒟⊂ℝd\mathcal{D}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a bounded domain. A function f:𝒟→ℝf:\mathcal{D}\to\mathbb{R} is MIP-representable on 𝒟\mathcal{D} if its graph restricted to 𝒟\mathcal{D} can be described exactly by a finite collection of linear constraints involving auxiliary continuous and integer variables. Equivalently, there exists a mixed integer linear feasible set whose projection onto the input-output coordinates is exactly

{(𝐱,t)∣t=f⁡(𝐱)}.\left\{(\mathbf{x},t)\mid t=f(\mathbf{x})\right\}.

We use the following standard exact representation of a ReLU unit.

Lemma A.1 (Exact ReLU encoding).

Let h=max⁡{0,a}h=\max\{0,a\}, where the pre-activation aa has finite bounds

a¯≤a≤a¯.\underline{a}\leq a\leq\overline{a}.

Assume a¯≤0≤a¯\underline{a}\leq 0\leq\overline{a}. Then the graph of the ReLU can be represented exactly using one binary variable z∈{0,1}z\in\{0,1\} and the linear constraints

h\displaystyle h ≥a,\displaystyle\geq a, (9)
h\displaystyle h ≥0,\displaystyle\geq 0, (10)
h\displaystyle h ≤a−a¯​(1−z),\displaystyle\leq a-\underline{a}(1-z), (11)
h\displaystyle h ≤a¯​z.\displaystyle\leq\overline{a}z. (12)

If the bounds imply that the ReLU is always active or always inactive, the binary variable can be removed and the ReLU can be replaced by a linear equality.

Proof.

Consider first the case z=0z=0. Constraint (12) gives h≤0h\leq 0, and constraint (10) gives h≥0h\geq 0. Hence h=0h=0. Constraint (9) then implies a≤0a\leq 0. Therefore the inactive case represents h=max⁡{0,a}=0h=\max\{0,a\}=0.

Now consider the case z=1z=1. Constraint (11) gives h≤ah\leq a, and constraint (9) gives h≥ah\geq a. Hence h=ah=a. Constraint (10) also implies a≥0a\geq 0. Therefore the active case represents h=max⁡{0,a}=ah=\max\{0,a\}=a.

The two cases together describe exactly the graph of the ReLU over the bounded interval [a¯,a¯][\underline{a},\overline{a}]. ∎

A.2 Proof of Proposition 3.1

Proof.

Fix an instance graph 𝒢\mathcal{G}. The graph encoder produces node embeddings and a global graph embedding. Since the encoder is evaluated before inference, these embeddings are constants inside the optimization problem.

The readout maps the binary decision vector 𝐲\mathbf{y} to an input feature vector 𝐳0​(𝐲)\mathbf{z}^{0}(\mathbf{y}) for the energy head. By construction, each component of the readout is either affine in 𝐲\mathbf{y} or admits an exact mixed integer linear representation using auxiliary variables. The graph of the readout can therefore be described by linear constraints together with integrality restrictions.

The energy head is a feed-forward ReLU network. Each layer applies an affine transformation followed by componentwise ReLU activations. The affine transformations are represented by linear equalities. Each ReLU activation is represented exactly by Lemma A.1, using valid lower and upper bounds on the corresponding pre-activation.

Combining the readout representation, the affine layer equations, the ReLU encodings, and the final linear output equation gives a finite mixed integer linear representation of the graph of

𝐲↦Eθ​(𝒢,𝐲).\mathbf{y}\mapsto E_{\theta}(\mathcal{G},\mathbf{y}).

Thus, for fixed 𝒢\mathcal{G}, the learned energy is MIP-representable. ∎

A.3 Proof of Corollary 3.2

Proof.

By Proposition 3.1, the learned energy Eθ​(𝒢,𝐲)E_{\theta}(\mathcal{G},\mathbf{y}) admits an exact mixed integer linear representation. The feasible set

𝒞={𝐲∈{0,1}|𝒱|∣𝐀y​𝐲≤𝐛y}\mathcal{C}=\left\{\mathbf{y}\in\{0,1\}^{|\mathcal{V}|}\mid\mathbf{A}_{y}\mathbf{y}\leq\mathbf{b}_{y}\right\}

is described by linear constraints and binary restrictions.

The inference problem can therefore be written as the mixed integer linear optimization problem

min𝐲,𝝃,e\displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{y},\boldsymbol{\xi},e} e\displaystyle e
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} e=Eθ​(𝒢,𝐲),\displaystyle e=E_{\theta}(\mathcal{G},\mathbf{y}),
𝐀y​𝐲≤𝐛y,\displaystyle\mathbf{A}_{y}\mathbf{y}\leq\mathbf{b}_{y},
𝐲∈{0,1}|𝒱|,\displaystyle\mathbf{y}\in\{0,1\}^{|\mathcal{V}|},

where 𝝃\boldsymbol{\xi} denotes all auxiliary readout and ReLU variables.

If 𝒞\mathcal{C} is nonempty and this optimization problem is solved to global optimality, the returned solution is feasible by construction and globally optimal with respect to the learned energy over 𝒞\mathcal{C}. If the solver is stopped early, any returned incumbent remains feasible, although it need not be globally optimal with respect to the learned energy. ∎

A.4 Proof of Corollary 3.3

Proof.

The learned parameters θ\theta define the energy function Eθ​(𝒢,𝐲)E_{\theta}(\mathcal{G},\mathbf{y}). This function does not depend on the particular deployment-time feasible region. The feasible region enters only through the constraints imposed during inference.

Let

𝒞test={𝐲∈{0,1}|𝒱|∣𝐀test​𝐲≤𝐛test}\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{test}}=\left\{\mathbf{y}\in\{0,1\}^{|\mathcal{V}|}\mid\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{test}}\mathbf{y}\leq\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{test}}\right\}

be a test-time feasible set obtained by adding, removing, or modifying linear constraints over the same decision variables. The same learned energy can be optimized over the modified feasible set by solving

𝐲⋆∈arg⁡min𝐲∈𝒞test​Eθ​(𝒢,𝐲).\mathbf{y}^{\star}\in\arg\min_{\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{test}}}E_{\theta}(\mathcal{G},\mathbf{y}).

Exactness of the mixed integer encoding requires valid finite bounds for all ReLU pre-activations over the feasible set used at inference. If 𝒞test\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{test}} is contained in the domain used to compute the original Big-M constants, the original bounds remain valid. If the feasible set is expanded or otherwise leaves that domain, the Big-M constants are recomputed by bound propagation over 𝒞test\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{test}}. This changes only the encoding constants and does not require retraining the neural model. ∎

A.5 Bound Tightening

The exact ReLU encoding requires valid lower and upper bounds on each pre-activation. In practice, these bounds are obtained using interval bound propagation through the assembled readout and energy head. Tighter bounds make the mixed integer linear representation stronger by reducing Big-M constants and removing ReLU binaries whose activation status is fixed. The bound computation used in the experiments is described in Appendix C.2.

A.6 Expressivity Beyond Factorized Linear Scoring

We next formalize why the nonlinear energy head can represent interactions that are impossible for additive per-variable scoring functions.

Definition A.2 (Factorized linear score).

A score over binary configurations is factorized linear if it decomposes additively over individual variables as

L⁡(𝐲)=b+∑iwi​yi.L(\mathbf{y})=b+\sum_{i}w_{i}y_{i}.

Such a score assigns a contribution to each selected variable independently of which other variables are selected.

Proposition A.2 (Expressivity beyond linear scoring).

Let

Q⁡(𝐲)=c+∑i=1nai​yi+∑(i,j)∈ℰqi​j​yi​yjQ(\mathbf{y})=c+\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}y_{i}+\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}}q_{ij}y_{i}y_{j}

be a quadratic real-valued function over binary variables 𝐲∈{0,1}n\mathbf{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n}. If the readout contains the binary variables 𝐲\mathbf{y}, or an affine representation from which they can be recovered, then a one-hidden-layer ReLU energy head with at most n+|ℰ|n+|\mathcal{E}| hidden units can represent Q⁡(𝐲)Q(\mathbf{y}) exactly on the binary domain. If the architecture includes skip connections from the readout input to the output layer, then |ℰ||\mathcal{E}| hidden units are sufficient. Moreover, no factorized linear score can represent a quadratic function with a nonzero interaction coefficient.

Proof.

For binary variables,

yi​yj=max⁡(0,yi+yj−1).y_{i}y_{j}=\max(0,y_{i}+y_{j}-1).

Thus each quadratic interaction can be represented by one ReLU unit with pre-activation yi+yj−1y_{i}+y_{j}-1. The linear terms can be represented using additional ReLU units since yi=max⁡(0,yi)y_{i}=\max(0,y_{i}) for yi∈{0,1}y_{i}\in\{0,1\}. The final linear layer combines these units with weights qi​jq_{ij} and aia_{i}, and adds the bias cc. Hence a one-hidden-layer ReLU network with at most n+|ℰ|n+|\mathcal{E}| hidden units represents QQ exactly on the binary domain.

To show that factorized linear scoring cannot represent nonzero interactions, fix all coordinates of 𝐲\mathbf{y} except yiy_{i} and yjy_{j}. For any factorized linear score

L⁡(𝐲)=b+∑ℓ=1nwℓ​yℓ,L(\mathbf{y})=b+\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}w_{\ell}y_{\ell},

the mixed finite difference with respect to coordinates ii and jj is

Δi​j​L=L⁡(𝐲11)−L⁡(𝐲10)−L⁡(𝐲01)+L⁡(𝐲00)=0,\Delta_{ij}L=L(\mathbf{y}^{11})-L(\mathbf{y}^{10})-L(\mathbf{y}^{01})+L(\mathbf{y}^{00})=0,

where 𝐲a​b\mathbf{y}^{ab} denotes the vector obtained by setting yi=ay_{i}=a and yj=by_{j}=b while keeping all other coordinates fixed. For the quadratic interaction qi​j​yi​yjq_{ij}y_{i}y_{j}, the same finite difference equals qi​jq_{ij}. Therefore, if qi​j≠0q_{ij}\neq 0, no factorized linear score can represent the function exactly. ∎

Proposition A.2 shows that the nonlinear energy head is not merely an implementation detail. It strictly enlarges the class of binary objectives representable by exact Neural-MIP inference beyond additive per-variable scoring.

Appendix B Benchmark Problem Formulations

We provide the complete MIP formulations for all three benchmarks. Instance generation procedures and dataset statistics are described in Appendix D.

B.1 Combinatorial Auctions (CA)

The combinatorial auction problem (Leyton-Brown et al., 2000) allocates a set of items 𝒞\mathcal{C} to a set of bids ℬ\mathcal{B} so as to maximize total revenue. Each bid b∈ℬb\in\mathcal{B} specifies a bundle 𝒩⁡(b)⊆𝒞\mathcal{N}(b)\subseteq\mathcal{C} together with a value pb>0p_{b}>0. Let yb∈{0,1}y_{b}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether bid bb is accepted. The resulting 0–1 packing formulation is

max𝐲∈{0,1}|ℬ|∑b∈ℬpbybs.t.∑b:c∈𝒩⁡(b)yb≤1∀c∈𝒞.\max_{\mathbf{y}\in\{0,1\}^{|\mathcal{B}|}}\;\;\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}p_{b}\,y_{b}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{b:\,c\in\mathcal{N}(b)}y_{b}\leq 1\quad\forall c\in\mathcal{C}. (13)

The packing constraints enforce that each item is allocated to at most one accepted bid. The problem is NP-hard in general (Leyton-Brown et al., 2000).

We generate CA instances using the arbitrary-relations generator of Leyton-Brown et al. (2000). We consider a custom CA training distribution with (|𝒞|,|ℬ|)=(100,175)(|\mathcal{C}|,|\mathcal{B}|)=(100,175) and evaluate cross-scale generalization on a harder test distribution with (|𝒞|,|ℬ|)=(100,250)(|\mathcal{C}|,|\mathcal{B}|)=(100,250). Exact reference solutions are generated with a time limit of 36003600 s per instance.

Graph encoding.

We represent each instance as a bipartite graph with item nodes 𝒞\mathcal{C} and bid nodes ℬ\mathcal{B}. An edge (c,b)(c,b) is present if and only if item cc belongs to bid bb, i.e., if Ac​b=1A_{cb}=1 in the incidence matrix 𝐀∈{0,1}|𝒞|×|ℬ|\mathbf{A}\in\{0,1\}^{|\mathcal{C}|\times|\mathcal{B}|}. Our encoder is therefore a bipartite message-passing neural network over constraint-side item nodes and variable-side bid nodes.

Features.

For CA, item-node features encode local participation statistics (e.g., item degree and dummy-item indicators), while bid-node features encode bid value, bundle size, value-per-item, and a structural conflict proxy derived from competing bids. Both node types additionally receive a small amount of repeated global context, such as instance density and average bid statistics. Edge features encode normalized incidence-level signals linking item popularity, bid value, and bundle size.

Readout.

Let 𝐡b\mathbf{h}_{b} and 𝐡c\mathbf{h}_{c} denote the final embeddings of bid bb and item cc, respectively. For each item, an auxiliary continuous variable ucu_{c} indicates whether it is occupied by at least one selected bid:

uc=𝕀[∑b:c∈𝒩⁡(b)yb≥1].u_{c}=\mathbb{I}\left[\sum_{b:\,c\in\mathcal{N}(b)}y_{b}\geq 1\right]. (14)

This relationship is represented exactly using

uc\displaystyle u_{c} ≤∑b:c∈𝒩⁡(b)yb,\displaystyle\leq\sum_{b:\,c\in\mathcal{N}(b)}y_{b}, ∀c∈𝒞,\displaystyle\forall c\in\mathcal{C}, (15)
uc\displaystyle u_{c} ≥yb,\displaystyle\geq y_{b}, ∀c∈𝒞,∀b:c∈𝒩⁡(b).\displaystyle\forall c\in\mathcal{C},\quad\forall b:\,c\in\mathcal{N}(b). (16)

The corresponding occupied-item embedding pool is

𝐡occ​(𝐲)=∑c∈𝒞uc​𝐡c.\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{occ}}(\mathbf{y})=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}u_{c}\mathbf{h}_{c}. (17)

The readout additionally includes the compact scalar-summary vector

𝐬CA​(𝐲)=[sbid,socc,sdummy,sconf,smass,svalue,sbundle,srisk],\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{CA}}(\mathbf{y})=\left[s_{\mathrm{bid}},s_{\mathrm{occ}},s_{\mathrm{dummy}},s_{\mathrm{conf}},s_{\mathrm{mass}},s_{\mathrm{value}},s_{\mathrm{bundle}},s_{\mathrm{risk}}\right], (18)

whose components are the selected-bid fraction, occupied-item fraction, occupied dummy-item fraction, conflicted-item fraction, normalized conflict mass, normalized selected-value sum, normalized selected-bundle-size sum, and normalized selected conflict-risk sum, respectively.

The complete CA readout is

𝐳CA0​(𝐲)=[∑b∈ℬyb​𝐡b,∑c∈𝒞uc​𝐡c,𝐬CA​(𝐲),𝐡𝒢].\mathbf{z}^{0}_{\mathrm{CA}}(\mathbf{y})=\left[\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}y_{b}\mathbf{h}_{b},\;\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}u_{c}\mathbf{h}_{c},\;\mathbf{s}_{\mathrm{CA}}(\mathbf{y}),\;\mathbf{h}_{\mathcal{G}}\right]. (19)

The first pool represents the accepted bids, while the second captures their consequences on the item side of the bipartite graph. The scalar summaries provide compact information about selection density, item occupancy, aggregate value, bundle size, and conflict structure.

B.2 Quadratic Knapsack (QKP)

The Quadratic Knapsack Problem (Pisinger, 2007) selects a subset of nn items to maximize a quadratic objective subject to a linear capacity constraint:

max⁡∑i=1n𝐲∈{0,1}n⁡pi​yi+∑i=1n∑j=i+1nQi​j​yi​yjs.t.∑i=1nwi​yi≤W,\max_{\mathbf{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\;\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\,y_{i}\;+\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=i+1}^{n}Q_{ij}\,y_{i}y_{j}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}\,y_{i}\leq W, (20)

where pip_{i} is the linear profit of item ii, Qi​jQ_{ij} is the pairwise interaction profit between items ii and jj, wiw_{i} is the weight of item ii, and WW is the knapsack capacity. The quadratic term captures both positive and negative interactions between co-selected items, which motivates learning an energy function over complete configurations rather than independent per-item scores.

We consider instances with n=150n=150 items and interaction density ρ=0.30\rho=0.30. Linear profits are sampled as pi∼𝒰⁡[0,10]p_{i}\sim\mathcal{U}[0,10], item weights as wi∼𝒰⁡[1,10]w_{i}\sim\mathcal{U}[1,10], and the knapsack capacity is set to W=0.5​∑iwiW=0.5\sum_{i}w_{i}. Pairwise interactions are obtained from a symmetric random matrix with off-diagonal entries drawn from 𝒰⁡[−2,8]\mathcal{U}[-2,8], which is then sparsified to the target density ρ\rho. Reference solutions are computed with Gurobi (Gurobi Optimization, LLC, 2023) using a time limit of 36003600 s per instance.

Graph encoding.

We represent each instance as a bipartite graph with item nodes II and interaction nodes PP. Each interaction node p=(i,j)∈Pp=(i,j)\in P corresponds to a nonzero upper-triangular pairwise coefficient Qi​jQ_{ij} with i<ji<j, and is connected to both item nodes ii and jj. This construction allows message passing to propagate pairwise interaction information into the item embeddings used by the downstream readout.

Features.

For QKP, item-node features encode linear profit, weight, interaction degree, and average interaction strength, together with repeated global context such as graph density and aggregate interaction scale. Interaction-node features encode the magnitude and sign of the pairwise term, along with simple summaries of the associated item weights and profits. Edge features transmit normalized interaction strength and capacity-relevant pair information.

Readout.

Each QKP instance is represented as a bipartite graph between item nodes ℐ\mathcal{I} and interaction nodes 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Each interaction node p=(i,j)∈𝒫p=(i,j)\in\mathcal{P} corresponds to a nonzero upper-triangular pairwise coefficient Qi​jQ_{ij} and is connected to item nodes ii and jj. The resulting item embeddings 𝐡i\mathbf{h}_{i} therefore encode both item-level attributes and information propagated from the quadratic interactions.

Let yi∈{0,1}y_{i}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether item ii is selected. In addition to the selected-item embedding pool, QKP uses the unselected-item pool

𝐡unsel​(𝐲)=∑i∈ℐ(1−yi)​𝐡i,\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{unsel}}(\mathbf{y})=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}(1-y_{i})\mathbf{h}_{i}, (21)

the selected-item fraction

rsel​(𝐲)=1|ℐ|​∑i∈ℐyi,r_{\mathrm{sel}}(\mathbf{y})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}y_{i}, (22)

and the normalized capacity usage

rcap​(𝐲)=1W​∑i∈ℐwi​yi.r_{\mathrm{cap}}(\mathbf{y})=\frac{1}{W}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}w_{i}y_{i}. (23)

The additional structured component is

𝐳linQKP​(𝐲)=[𝐡unsel​(𝐲),rsel​(𝐲),rcap​(𝐲)].\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{lin}}^{\mathrm{QKP}}(\mathbf{y})=\left[\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{unsel}}(\mathbf{y}),\;r_{\mathrm{sel}}(\mathbf{y}),\;r_{\mathrm{cap}}(\mathbf{y})\right]. (24)

The complete QKP readout is

𝐳QKP0​(𝐲)=[∑i∈ℐyi​𝐡i,∑i∈ℐ(1−yi)​𝐡i,1|ℐ|​∑i∈ℐyi,1W​∑i∈ℐwi​yi,𝐡𝒢].\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{QKP}}^{0}(\mathbf{y})=\left[\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}y_{i}\mathbf{h}_{i},\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}(1-y_{i})\mathbf{h}_{i},\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}y_{i},\;\frac{1}{W}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}w_{i}y_{i},\;\mathbf{h}_{\mathcal{G}}\right]. (25)

The selected- and unselected-item pools expose information about both sides of the current partition of the item set. The two scalar summaries describe the size of the selected set and its consumption of the available knapsack capacity. All four decision-dependent components are affine in 𝐲\mathbf{y}.

B.3 Personalized Medicine Supply Chain (CART)

The personalized medicine supply chain problem optimizes the strategic selection of cell therapy manufacturing facilities and the routing of patient therapies through a multi-echelon logistics network under strict capacity and turnaround-time constraints (Triantafyllou et al., 2022).

Problem structure.

The problem decomposes naturally into two levels:

  • •

    Strategic master problem: select which subset of |ℳ||\mathcal{M}| candidate manufacturing facilities to open. This involves |ℳ||\mathcal{M}| binary variables ym∈{0,1}y_{m}\in\{0,1\}.

  • •

    Operational subproblem: given open facilities, route all patient therapies through the network to minimize total cost subject to capacity and timing constraints. This involves continuous and binary flow variables but becomes tractable once the facility set is fixed.

The monolithic MILP is intractable at scale because the number of patient routing variables grows as |P|×|C|×|M|×|J|×|T||P|\times|C|\times|M|\times|J|\times|T|, which reaches millions for realistic instances. EnerGNN learns an energy over facility location configurations 𝐲={ym}\mathbf{y}=\{y_{m}\} which is then optimized under the strategic feasibility constraints; the operational subproblem induced by the selected configuration is subsequently solved exactly by Gurobi.

Full MILP formulation.

We provide the detailed mixed integer linear programming (MILP) formulation for the personalized medicine CAR T-cell therapy supply chain problem. The model jointly optimizes facility location, patient assignment, and time-dependent logistics under capacity and turnaround-time constraints.

Sets and indices

Let 𝒫\mathcal{P}, 𝒞\mathcal{C}, ℳ\mathcal{M}, ℋ\mathcal{H}, 𝒥\mathcal{J}, and 𝒯\mathcal{T} denote the sets of patients, clinical leukapheresis sites, candidate manufacturing facilities, hospitals, transportation modes, and discrete time periods, respectively. Indices are denoted by pp, cc, mm, hh, jj, and tt.

Parameters
  • •

    CminvC^{\mathrm{inv}}_{m}: capital investment cost for opening manufacturing facility mm.

  • •

    CmfixC^{\mathrm{fix}}_{m}: fixed operating cost of facility mm.

  • •

    CpvarC^{\mathrm{var}}_{p}: patient-specific variable manufacturing cost.

  • •

    CqcC^{\mathrm{qc}}: quality-control cost per therapy.

  • •

    KmK_{m}: maximum processing capacity, or number of parallel manufacturing lines, at facility mm.

  • •

    δp​c​t\delta_{pct}: binary parameter equal to 1 if patient pp arrives at clinical site cc at time tt.

  • •

    τlp\tau^{\mathrm{lp}}: duration of leukapheresis.

  • •

    τman\tau^{\mathrm{man}}: duration of manufacturing.

  • •

    τqc\tau^{\mathrm{qc}}: duration of quality control.

  • •

    τjout\tau^{\mathrm{out}}_{j}: transportation time from a clinical site to a manufacturing facility using mode jj.

  • •

    τjret\tau^{\mathrm{ret}}_{j}: transportation time from a manufacturing facility to a hospital using mode jj.

  • •

    Cc​m​joutC^{\mathrm{out}}_{cmj}: transportation cost from clinical site cc to facility mm using mode jj.

  • •

    Cm​h​jretC^{\mathrm{ret}}_{mhj}: transportation cost from facility mm to hospital hh using mode jj.

  • •

    BB: maximum number of manufacturing facilities that can be opened.

  • •

    DD: maximum allowable vein-to-vein turnaround time.

  • •

    NPN_{P}: total number of patients in the planning horizon.

Variables with time indices outside 𝒯\mathcal{T} are fixed to zero.

Decision variables

Facility location variables.

ym∈{0,1},∀m∈ℳ,y_{m}\in\{0,1\},\qquad\forall m\in\mathcal{M},

where ym=1y_{m}=1 if manufacturing facility mm is opened.

Network design variables.

uc​m∈{0,1},∀c∈𝒞,m∈ℳ,u_{cm}\in\{0,1\},\qquad\forall c\in\mathcal{C},\,m\in\mathcal{M},

where uc​m=1u_{cm}=1 if clinical site cc is connected to manufacturing facility mm.

vm​h∈{0,1},∀m∈ℳ,h∈ℋ,v_{mh}\in\{0,1\},\qquad\forall m\in\mathcal{M},\,h\in\mathcal{H},

where vm​h=1v_{mh}=1 if manufacturing facility mm is connected to hospital hh.

Transportation variables.

xp​c​m​j​t∈{0,1},∀p∈𝒫,c∈𝒞,m∈ℳ,j∈𝒥,t∈𝒯,x_{pcmjt}\in\{0,1\},\qquad\forall p\in\mathcal{P},\,c\in\mathcal{C},\,m\in\mathcal{M},\,j\in\mathcal{J},\,t\in\mathcal{T},

where xp​c​m​j​t=1x_{pcmjt}=1 if patient pp’s material is transported from clinical site cc to facility mm using mode jj at time tt.

wp​m​h​j​t∈{0,1},∀p∈𝒫,m∈ℳ,h∈ℋ,j∈𝒥,t∈𝒯,w_{pmhjt}\in\{0,1\},\qquad\forall p\in\mathcal{P},\,m\in\mathcal{M},\,h\in\mathcal{H},\,j\in\mathcal{J},\,t\in\mathcal{T},

where wp​m​h​j​t=1w_{pmhjt}=1 if therapy pp is transported from facility mm to hospital hh using mode jj at time tt.

Flow variables.

ℓp​c​m​j​tdep≥0,ℓp​c​m​j​tarr≥0,\ell^{\mathrm{dep}}_{pcmjt}\geq 0,\qquad\ell^{\mathrm{arr}}_{pcmjt}\geq 0,

denote, respectively, material leaving clinical site cc for facility mm, and material arriving at facility mm, for patient pp, mode jj, and time tt.

qp​m​tin≥0,qp​m​tout≥0,q^{\mathrm{in}}_{pmt}\geq 0,\qquad q^{\mathrm{out}}_{pmt}\geq 0,

denote, respectively, therapy pp entering and leaving manufacturing facility mm at time tt.

gp​c​tout≥0,gp​h​tin≥0,g^{\mathrm{out}}_{pct}\geq 0,\qquad g^{\mathrm{in}}_{pht}\geq 0,

denote, respectively, material leaving clinical site cc, and final therapy arriving at hospital hh, for patient pp at time tt.

Timing variables.

sp,ep,rp≥0,∀p∈𝒫,s_{p},e_{p},r_{p}\geq 0,\qquad\forall p\in\mathcal{P},

denote the start time, completion time, and turnaround time of patient pp.

Objective function

The objective minimizes total supply chain cost, including facility investment, fixed operating cost, patient-specific manufacturing cost, quality control, and transportation:

minZ=\displaystyle\min\quad Z= ∑m∈ℳ(Cminv+Cmfix)​ym+∑p∈𝒫(Cpvar+Cqc)\displaystyle\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}}\left(C^{\mathrm{inv}}_{m}+C^{\mathrm{fix}}_{m}\right)y_{m}+\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\left(C^{\mathrm{var}}_{p}+C^{\mathrm{qc}}\right) (26)
+∑p∈𝒫∑c∈𝒞∑m∈ℳ∑j∈𝒥∑t∈𝒯Coutc​m​jxp​c​m​j​t\displaystyle+\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}C^{\mathrm{out}}_{cmj}x_{pcmjt}
+∑p∈𝒫∑m∈ℳ∑h∈ℋ∑j∈𝒥∑t∈𝒯Cretm​h​jwp​m​h​j​t.\displaystyle+\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}}\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}C^{\mathrm{ret}}_{mhj}w_{pmhjt}.

Equivalently, if facility investment and fixed operating costs are allocated per patient as in the original implementation, the patient-level manufacturing cost may be written as

Cpman=∑m∈ℳ(Cminv+Cmfix)​ymNP+Cpvar,∀p∈𝒫.C^{\mathrm{man}}_{p}=\frac{\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}}\left(C^{\mathrm{inv}}_{m}+C^{\mathrm{fix}}_{m}\right)y_{m}}{N_{P}}+C^{\mathrm{var}}_{p},\qquad\forall p\in\mathcal{P}. (27)
Constraints

Leukapheresis completion. A patient sample can leave the clinical site only after the leukapheresis duration has elapsed:

gp​c,t+τlpout=δp​c​t,∀p∈𝒫,c∈𝒞,t∈𝒯.g^{\mathrm{out}}_{pc,t+\tau^{\mathrm{lp}}}=\delta_{pct},\qquad\forall p\in\mathcal{P},\,c\in\mathcal{C},\,t\in\mathcal{T}. (28)

Outbound shipment selection. Each patient is assigned to exactly one outbound shipment:

∑c∈𝒞∑m∈ℳ∑j∈𝒥∑t∈𝒯xp​c​m​j​t=1,∀p∈𝒫.\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}x_{pcmjt}=1,\qquad\forall p\in\mathcal{P}. (29)

The outbound shipment variables define the material leaving the clinical site:

ℓp​c​m​j​tdep=xp​c​m​j​t,∀p,c,m,j,t.\ell^{\mathrm{dep}}_{pcmjt}=x_{pcmjt},\qquad\forall p,c,m,j,t. (30)

All material leaving a clinical site must be assigned to a manufacturing facility and a transportation mode:

gp​c​tout=∑m∈ℳ∑j∈𝒥ℓp​c​m​j​tdep,∀p,c,t.g^{\mathrm{out}}_{pct}=\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\ell^{\mathrm{dep}}_{pcmjt},\qquad\forall p,c,t. (31)

Outbound transportation timing. Material arriving at the manufacturing facility is delayed by the transportation time of the selected mode:

ℓp​c​m​j,t+τjoutarr=ℓp​c​m​j​tdep,∀p,c,m,j,t.\ell^{\mathrm{arr}}_{pcmj,t+\tau^{\mathrm{out}}_{j}}=\ell^{\mathrm{dep}}_{pcmjt},\qquad\forall p,c,m,j,t. (32)

The total material entering a manufacturing facility equals all arrivals from clinical sites:

qp​m​tin=∑c∈𝒞∑j∈𝒥ℓp​c​m​j​tarr,∀p,m,t.q^{\mathrm{in}}_{pmt}=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\ell^{\mathrm{arr}}_{pcmjt},\qquad\forall p,m,t. (33)

Manufacturing and quality control timing. A therapy can leave the manufacturing facility only after manufacturing and quality control are completed:

qp​m,t+τman+τqcout=qp​m​tin,∀p,m,t.q^{\mathrm{out}}_{pm,t+\tau^{\mathrm{man}}+\tau^{\mathrm{qc}}}=q^{\mathrm{in}}_{pmt},\qquad\forall p,m,t. (34)

Return shipment after manufacturing. Every completed therapy must be assigned to exactly one return shipment:

∑h∈ℋ∑j∈𝒥wp​m​h​j​t=qp​m​tout,∀p,m,t.\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}w_{pmhjt}=q^{\mathrm{out}}_{pmt},\qquad\forall p,m,t. (35)

Hospital arrival timing. The final therapy arrives at the hospital after the return transportation delay:

gp​h,t+τjretin=∑m∈ℳwp​m​h​j​t,∀p,h,j,t.g^{\mathrm{in}}_{ph,t+\tau^{\mathrm{ret}}_{j}}=\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}}w_{pmhjt},\qquad\forall p,h,j,t. (36)

Each patient receives exactly one final therapy delivery:

∑h∈ℋ∑t∈𝒯gp​h​tin=1,∀p∈𝒫.\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}g^{\mathrm{in}}_{pht}=1,\qquad\forall p\in\mathcal{P}. (37)

Manufacturing capacity. The number of therapies simultaneously occupying facility mm cannot exceed the installed capacity:

∑p∈𝒫(∑τ=0tqp​m​τin−∑τ=0tqp​m​τout)≤Km​ym,∀m∈ℳ,t∈𝒯.\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\left(\sum_{\tau=0}^{t}q^{\mathrm{in}}_{pm\tau}-\sum_{\tau=0}^{t}q^{\mathrm{out}}_{pm\tau}\right)\leq K_{m}y_{m},\qquad\forall m\in\mathcal{M},\,t\in\mathcal{T}. (38)

Network design and facility activation. A clinical site can only be connected to an opened manufacturing facility:

uc​m≤ym,∀c∈𝒞,m∈ℳ.u_{cm}\leq y_{m},\qquad\forall c\in\mathcal{C},\,m\in\mathcal{M}. (39)

A manufacturing facility can only be connected to a hospital if the facility is opened:

vm​h≤ym,∀m∈ℳ,h∈ℋ.v_{mh}\leq y_{m},\qquad\forall m\in\mathcal{M},\,h\in\mathcal{H}. (40)

Outbound shipments are allowed only along selected clinical-site-to-facility links:

xp​c​m​j​t≤uc​m,∀p,c,m,j,t.x_{pcmjt}\leq u_{cm},\qquad\forall p,c,m,j,t. (41)

Return shipments are allowed only along selected facility-to-hospital links:

wp​m​h​j​t≤vm​h,∀p,m,h,j,t.w_{pmhjt}\leq v_{mh},\qquad\forall p,m,h,j,t. (42)

The total number of established manufacturing facilities is bounded:

∑m∈ℳym≤B.\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}}y_{m}\leq B. (43)

Start, completion, and turnaround times. The start time of each patient is determined by the clinical site arrival time:

sp=∑c∈𝒞∑t∈𝒯t​δp​c​t,∀p∈𝒫.s_{p}=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}t\,\delta_{pct},\qquad\forall p\in\mathcal{P}. (44)

The completion time is the arrival time of the final therapy at the hospital:

ep=∑h∈ℋ∑t∈𝒯t​gp​h​tin,∀p∈𝒫.e_{p}=\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}t\,g^{\mathrm{in}}_{pht},\qquad\forall p\in\mathcal{P}. (45)

Turnaround time is defined as the time between patient arrival and therapy delivery:

rp=ep−sp,∀p∈𝒫.r_{p}=e_{p}-s_{p},\qquad\forall p\in\mathcal{P}. (46)

The vein-to-vein turnaround time must not exceed the clinical deadline:

rp≤D,∀p∈𝒫.r_{p}\leq D,\qquad\forall p\in\mathcal{P}. (47)

Graph encoding.

We represent each instance as a complete bipartite graph between clinical facility-demand nodes 𝒞\mathcal{C} and candidate manufacturing facility nodes ℳ\mathcal{M}. Demand-node features summarize the local patient arrival profile at each clinical site using aggregate demand statistics, including total demand, variability, peak demand, empirical quantiles, and seasonal Fourier components. Facility node features encode normalized capacity, operating cost rate, and demand-weighted transport statistics. Each edge (c,m)(c,m) encodes the transport cost between clinical site cc and facility mm using a normalized scalar together with an RBF expansion. This compressed graph representation exposes the aggregate operational structure of the full supply chain without explicitly instantiating patient-level routing variables in the learned model.

Features.

In the implementation used for our experiments, demand-node features have dimension 14 and include local demand statistics together with a small amount of repeated global context. Facility node features have dimension 9 and encode capacity, normalized fixed cost rate, and transport summaries, again augmented with repeated global context. Edge features have dimension 6, consisting of one normalized transport cost feature and a five-dimensional RBF expansion.

Readout.

Each CART instance is represented as a complete bipartite graph

𝒢CART=(𝒞∪ℳ,ℰ),ℰ=𝒞×ℳ,\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{CART}}=(\mathcal{C}\cup\mathcal{M},\mathcal{E}),\qquad\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{M},

where 𝒞\mathcal{C} denotes clinical facility-demand nodes and ℳ\mathcal{M} denotes candidate manufacturing-facility nodes. The encoder returns demand-node embeddings 𝐡c\mathbf{h}_{c}, facility-node embeddings 𝐡m\mathbf{h}_{m}, and a global graph embedding 𝐡𝒢\mathbf{h}_{\mathcal{G}}.

Let ym∈{0,1}y_{m}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether manufacturing facility mm is selected. For each demand node cc, an auxiliary binary variable qcq_{c} indicates whether it is covered by at least one selected facility:

qc=𝕀[∑m∈ℳ⁡(c)ym≥1],q_{c}=\mathbb{I}\left[\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}(c)}y_{m}\geq 1\right], (48)

where ℳ⁡(c)\mathcal{M}(c) is the set of candidate facilities connected to demand node cc. This logical relationship is represented exactly through

qc\displaystyle q_{c} ≤∑m∈ℳ⁡(c)ym,\displaystyle\leq\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}(c)}y_{m}, ∀c∈𝒞,\displaystyle\forall c\in\mathcal{C}, (49)
qc\displaystyle q_{c} ≥ym,\displaystyle\geq y_{m}, ∀c∈𝒞,∀m∈ℳ⁡(c).\displaystyle\forall c\in\mathcal{C},\quad\forall m\in\mathcal{M}(c). (50)

The additional decision-dependent component is the pooled embedding of the covered demand nodes:

𝐳linCART​(𝐲)=∑c∈𝒞qc​𝐡c.\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{lin}}^{\mathrm{CART}}(\mathbf{y})=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}q_{c}\mathbf{h}_{c}. (51)

The complete CART readout is therefore

𝐳CART0​(𝐲)=[∑m∈ℳym​𝐡m,∑c∈𝒞qc​𝐡c,𝐡𝒢].\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{CART}}^{0}(\mathbf{y})=\left[\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}}y_{m}\mathbf{h}_{m},\;\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}q_{c}\mathbf{h}_{c},\;\mathbf{h}_{\mathcal{G}}\right]. (52)

The first term represents the selected manufacturing facilities, while the second represents the clinical facility-demand nodes covered by the selected facility set. CART therefore uses pooled learned embeddings from both sides of the bipartite graph and does not include additional manually constructed scalar summaries.

Appendix C Neural-MIP Encoding

We encode the learned ReLU energy head exactly inside the MIP using a standard Big-M formulation for ReLU activations. The benchmark-specific combinatorial constraints and the readout-level auxiliary variables are then combined with this head encoding to yield the final inference model.

C.1 ReLU Head Encoding

Let

ajl=𝐰j⊤​𝐡l−1+bja_{j}^{l}=\mathbf{w}_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{h}^{l-1}+b_{j}

denote the affine pre-activation of neuron jj in layer ll, and let

hjl=max⁡(0,ajl)h_{j}^{l}=\max(0,a_{j}^{l})

be the corresponding ReLU activation. Suppose valid finite bounds

a¯jl≤ajl≤a¯jl\underline{a}_{j}^{l}\leq a_{j}^{l}\leq\overline{a}_{j}^{l}

are available. For neurons whose bounds satisfy a¯jl<0<a¯jl\underline{a}_{j}^{l}<0<\overline{a}_{j}^{l}, we introduce a binary activation indicator zjl∈{0,1}z_{j}^{l}\in\{0,1\} and impose the exact mixed integer linear formulation

hjl\displaystyle h_{j}^{l} ≥ajl,\displaystyle\geq a_{j}^{l}, (53)
hjl\displaystyle h_{j}^{l} ≥0,\displaystyle\geq 0, (54)
hjl\displaystyle h_{j}^{l} ≤ajl−a¯jl​(1−zjl),\displaystyle\leq a_{j}^{l}-\underline{a}_{j}^{l}(1-z_{j}^{l}), (55)
hjl\displaystyle h_{j}^{l} ≤a¯jl​zjl.\displaystyle\leq\overline{a}_{j}^{l}z_{j}^{l}. (56)

If a¯jl≥0\underline{a}_{j}^{l}\geq 0, the neuron is always active and we set hjl=ajlh_{j}^{l}=a_{j}^{l}. If a¯jl≤0\overline{a}_{j}^{l}\leq 0, the neuron is always inactive and we set hjl=0h_{j}^{l}=0. The final linear layer is encoded by linear equality constraints, producing the scalar energy minimized by the inference MIP.

C.2 Interval Bound Propagation

The practical strength of the Neural-MIP depends on the tightness of the pre-activation bounds. We obtain these bounds using interval bound propagation through the assembled readout and energy head.

For an affine layer

𝐚l=Wl​𝐡l−1+𝐛l\mathbf{a}^{l}=W^{l}\mathbf{h}^{l-1}+\mathbf{b}^{l}

with elementwise input bounds [𝐡¯l−1,𝐡¯l−1][\underline{\mathbf{h}}^{\,l-1},\overline{\mathbf{h}}^{\,l-1}], the pre-activation bounds are

a¯jl\displaystyle\underline{a}_{j}^{l} =bjl+∑imin⁡(Wj​il​h¯il−1,Wj​il​h¯il−1),\displaystyle=b_{j}^{l}+\sum_{i}\min\!\left(W_{ji}^{l}\underline{h}_{i}^{\,l-1},W_{ji}^{l}\overline{h}_{i}^{\,l-1}\right), (57)
a¯jl\displaystyle\overline{a}_{j}^{l} =bjl+∑imax⁡(Wj​il​h¯il−1,Wj​il​h¯il−1).\displaystyle=b_{j}^{l}+\sum_{i}\max\!\left(W_{ji}^{l}\underline{h}_{i}^{\,l-1},W_{ji}^{l}\overline{h}_{i}^{\,l-1}\right). (58)

The corresponding post-ReLU bounds are

h¯jl=max⁡(0,a¯jl),h¯jl=max⁡(0,a¯jl).\underline{h}_{j}^{l}=\max(0,\underline{a}_{j}^{l}),\qquad\overline{h}_{j}^{l}=\max(0,\overline{a}_{j}^{l}).

These pre-activation bounds are used directly in the exact ReLU formulation above. When the bounds imply a fixed activation state, the corresponding binary variable is removed. Overall, the benchmark-specific readout linearizations and subsequent interval propagation provide the neuron-wise pre-activation bounds used in exact MIP inference.

C.3 Benchmark-Specific Input Bounds

The input intervals for this propagation step are derived from the exact linearized readout features used by each benchmark.

CART.

For CART, the readout combines pooled selected facility embeddings, pooled covered-demand embeddings, and a global graph embedding. Bounds for the selected-facility pooling terms are obtained from the facility cardinality constraints kmin≤‖𝐲‖1≤kmaxk_{\min}\leq\|\mathbf{y}\|_{1}\leq k_{\max}. Coverage terms are linearized using auxiliary binary variables indicating whether each demand node is served by at least one selected facility, and their bounds are computed from sign-split sums over the corresponding coefficients.

CA.

For CA, the readout includes pooled selected bid and occupied item embeddings together with scalar summaries such as selected bid fraction, occupied item fraction, and aggregate selected bid statistics. These are encoded with auxiliary continuous occupancy variables and count-based one-hot linearizations, which allow exact bounds to be propagated through the resulting MLP input.

QKP.

For QKP, the readout pools selected item embeddings and, in the size-aware variant, also includes unselected item summaries, selected fraction, and used capacity mass. Under the knapsack constraint, selected pool bounds are tightened using a fractional knapsack relaxation rather than naive unconstrained cardinality intervals. This yields substantially tighter input bounds for the downstream ReLU encoding.

Overall, the benchmark-specific readout linearizations and the subsequent interval propagation provide the neuron-wise Big-M constants used in exact MIP inference.

Beyond the energy encoding, the following hard constraints are added to the inference MIP for each benchmark:

CART.

∑mκm​ym\displaystyle\sum_{m}\kappa_{m}y_{m} ≥κref,\displaystyle\geq\kappa_{\mathrm{ref}}, (60)
yj\displaystyle y_{j} ≤yi∀(i,j)∈𝒮.\displaystyle\leq y_{i}\qquad\forall(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}. (61)

where (59) opens at most kmaxk_{\max} facilities, (60) requires total open capacity to meet the peak reference demand κref\kappa_{\mathrm{ref}}, and (61) imposes symmetry-breaking cuts over pairs of identical capacity facilities 𝒮\mathcal{S}.

∑b:c∈𝒩⁡(b)yb≤1∀c∈𝒞.\displaystyle\sum_{b:c\in\mathcal{N}(b)}y_{b}\leq 1\qquad\forall c\in\mathcal{C}. (62)
