∑iwi​yi≤W\displaystyle\sum_{i}w_{i}y_{i}\leq W (63)

where (63) enforces that the total selected weight remains within the budget WW.

Appendix D Dataset Splits and Candidate Pool Construction

Dataset splits.

For each benchmark, we use 800 training instances, 100 validation instances, and 100 held-out test instances.

For each training instance, we construct a candidate pool 𝒴=ℱ∪ℐ\mathcal{Y}=\mathcal{F}\cup\mathcal{I} containing feasible and infeasible configurations. Pool construction is benchmark-specific.

CART. For CART, each instance has 16 candidate facilities. We first solve the unrestricted patient-level MIP to global optimality and collect incumbent facility selection configurations from branch-and-bound. Additional candidates are generated using capacity- and transport-guided heuristics, local Hamming perturbations, swaps, facility additions and removals, and random configurations with varying cardinality. Each candidate is evaluated by solving the corresponding tactical patient scheduling MIP. Feasible configurations attaining the proven global optimum within numerical tolerance are labeled positive, other feasible configurations are labeled feasible negatives, and configurations certified infeasible are labeled infeasible negatives. We retain 160 candidates per instance through stratified selection, initially keeping up to three positives and targeting 30% infeasible negatives among the remaining candidates.

CA. For CA, we first solve each instance with Gurobi and collect incumbent solutions from branch-and-bound. Feasible solutions with relative primal gap at most ϵpos=0.01\epsilon_{\text{pos}}=0.01 are labelled positive, up to a maximum of 50 positives per instance. We then construct 64 feasible negatives using a quota-driven mixture of additional incumbent solutions, guided local Hamming perturbations, and farther Hamming perturbations of the best solution. The feasible-negative selection is balanced across Hamming distance buckets and primal gap bands. Finally, we generate 50 infeasible negatives by perturbing feasible masks into different violation bands, corresponding to mild, moderate, and severe item conflicts.

QKP. For QKP, we impose a one-hour time limit on Gurobi per instance. Training and validation may include instances for which global optimality is not certified within this limit. In contrast, the test set contains instances with Gurobi certified global optima, allowing all reported primal gaps to be measured against proven optimal solutions. For each training instance, we retain the best available solution together with all incumbent solutions whose relative primal gap is at most ϵpos=0.01\epsilon_{\text{pos}}=0.01; these form the positive subset. We then generate 128 feasible negatives and 64 infeasible negatives using stochastic mask proposals. Each proposal is either a random binary mask with random density or a mutation of the best mask obtained by flipping a random subset of items. Proposed masks that satisfy the knapsack constraint are retained as feasible negatives, while those that violate the capacity constraint are retained as infeasible negatives.

D.1 Offline Computational Cost and Amortization

The main benchmark runtimes report the online inference and optimization phase. EnerGNN also incurs a one-time offline cost for solver-based candidate generation and neural model training. Table 6 reports the complete elapsed wall-clock cost of this offline phase. Candidate generation was distributed across 1000 submitted jobs, with approximately 80 jobs running concurrently, subject to scheduler availability. Reported elapsed wall-clock times include queueing effects and therefore depend on cluster availability.

For a benchmark where EnerGNN is faster online than solving the full problem, the approximate number of deployment instances required to recover the offline investment is calculated as

Nbreak−even=TofflineTfull−TEnerGNN,N_{\mathrm{break-even}}=\frac{T_{\mathrm{offline}}}{T_{\mathrm{full}}-T_{\mathrm{EnerGNN}}},

where TofflineT_{\mathrm{offline}} includes label generation and training, TfullT_{\mathrm{full}} is the mean time required to solve a new instance using the original optimisation formulation, and TEnerGNNT_{\mathrm{EnerGNN}} is the mean online EnerGNN time.

The offline investment is recovered after approximately 125 QKP instances and 130 CART instances under the reported experimental conditions. No break-even point is reported for CA because Gurobi is already faster on the original auction formulation. These results make explicit that EnerGNN is intended for repeated decision-making settings in which the one-time solver supervision and training costs can be amortised across many deployment instances.

D.2 Computational Setup

Experiments were conducted using the Imperial College London CX3 high-performance computing cluster and a local workstation. Training, validation, and test datasets were generated on CPU nodes with up to 250 GB of RAM. Neural models were trained offline on GPU nodes equipped with NVIDIA Quadro RTX 6000 GPUs, using one GPU, 4 CPU cores, and 24 GB of RAM. Test time optimization and Neural-MIP inference were performed on a workstation with 64 GB of RAM. Optimization runs used Gurobi 12.0.2.

Reported runtimes exclude dataset generation, candidate pool construction, and neural network training. For learning-based methods, reported online times include neural prediction or encoding, construction of the corresponding optimization problem, and all solver calls required to produce the final solution.

Appendix E Loss Configuration Details

E.1 Loss Configuration Used in Reported Experiments

All reported experiments use the same loss formulation, consisting of an optimality-aware contrastive loss term, a feasible calibration term, and an infeasibility shaping term. The optimality-aware contrastive term is applied over the full candidate pool. Across these runs, we use a bipartite MPNN encoder with hidden dimension 128, two message-passing rounds, and dropout 0.1. The reported runs use a shallow MLP energy head with one hidden layer of width 32.

E.2 Training and Model Selection

All models are trained using Adam with the benchmark-specific hyperparameters reported in Table 7. Model selection is performed on the validation set. For each run, we retain the checkpoint with the lowest validation mean primal gap and report final test results from this checkpoint.

Adaptive Huber scale.

For each candidate pool, the Huber transition scale is computed as

δℱ=min⁡{δmax,max⁡[δmin,κδ​(maxi∈ℱ⁡gi−mini∈ℱ⁡gi)]}.\delta_{\mathcal{F}}=\min\!\left\{\delta_{\max},\;\max\!\left[\delta_{\min},\;\kappa_{\delta}\left(\max_{i\in\mathcal{F}}g_{i}-\min_{i\in\mathcal{F}}g_{i}\right)\right]\right\}. (64)

Appendix F Scale of the CART Formulation

The number of strategic variables alone understates the computational scale of the CART benchmark. Each strategic facility selection controls a large patient-level assignment and scheduling formulation. Across the 100 test instances with m=16m=16, the dimensions of the complete monolithic formulations are reported in Table 8.

EnerGNN selects 3.21 of the 16 candidate manufacturing facilities on average. Fixing the strategic facility set substantially reduces the induced patient-level scheduling formulations, as shown in Table 9.

The numbers of constraints, binary variables, continuous variables, and total variables are reduced by approximately 77% on average. The number of general integer variables changes very little because these variables are primarily associated with patients and scheduling periods rather than with the candidate manufacturing facilities.

Appendix G Primal Gap Distributions

Figure 3 shows the primal gap distribution across test instances for all learning-based methods on each benchmark. The x-axis uses a log scale to show both near zero and high gap distributions simultaneously. EnerGNN maintains a tight distribution near zero across all three benchmarks, confirming that the means reported in Table 1 are representative. Primal gaps are computed relative to the global optimum.

Appendix H Additional Zero-Shot Constraint Injection Results

We provide additional zero-shot constraint injection experiments in which the trained energy is unchanged and only the feasible region of the inference MIP is modified. In CART, cardinality and facility activation constraints restrict the available strategic configurations. We use the linear head EnerGNN model for CA, as it achieved the best performance in the main experiments. Optimality gaps are measured relative to reference optima computed under the same injected constraints. These experiments complement the stronger constraint shifts reported in Section 4, where variables selected in the original optimal solution are explicitly made unavailable.

Appendix I Cross-scale Generalization with Nonlinear Energy Head on Combinatorial Auctions

For CA, the main paper reports cross-scale generalization using the linear head variant of EnerGNN, which achieves the best performance on this benchmark. For completeness, Table 12 reports the corresponding results using the nonlinear ReLU energy head, evaluated without retraining.

Appendix J Ablation Study Details

J.1 Energy Head Architecture Ablation

We evaluate the effect of energy head width and depth on QKP and CART. In all cases, the resulting Neural-MIP is solved to global optimality with respect to the learned energy. Increasing the width or depth of the embedded ReLU head adds activation binaries to the inference MIP. Across both benchmarks, larger heads do not systematically improve solution quality, while deeper and wider architectures can substantially increase solution time.

For QKP, increasing head capacity does not consistently improve solution quality. For example, the one-layer width-16 model achieves a 0.47% mean gap in 1.07 s, while the two-layer width-64 model achieves a similar 0.37% gap but requires 186.23 s. The same pattern appears in CART. Increasing from a one-layer width-16 head to a two-layer width-64 head raises inference time from 0.59 s to 24.69 s, while the mean gap changes only from 0.09% to 0.07%.

These results illustrate the expressiveness–tractability trade-off of the Neural-MIP formulation. Increasing the capacity of the embedded energy head adds ReLU binaries and can substantially increase solution time without a corresponding improvement in solution quality. Importantly, the GNN encoder is evaluated before optimization and is therefore not part of the inference MIP. Representational capacity can consequently be placed primarily in the graph encoder while keeping the optimization-compatible energy head compact.

J.2 Loss Variant Ablation

We evaluate three loss configurations on each benchmark:

  • •

    Full loss: all three components active (ℒcon+ℒcal+ℒinf\mathcal{L}_{\text{con}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{cal}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{inf}}).

  • •

    No primal gap term: λcal=0\lambda_{\text{cal}}=0, contrastive and infeasibility only.

  • •

    No infeasibility term: λinf=0\lambda_{\text{inf}}=0, contrastive and calibration only.

J.3 Strict Feasible–Infeasible Dominance

The standard training objective does not enforce that every feasible candidate must have lower energy than every infeasible candidate. To test whether such a complete ordering would be beneficial, we evaluate a stricter alternative. Let

EmaxF=maxi∈ℱ⁡Eθ​(G,𝐲i)E_{\max}^{F}=\max_{i\in\mathcal{F}}E_{\theta}(G,\mathbf{y}_{i})

denote the highest feasible energy in the current candidate pool. During backpropagation, EmaxFE_{\max}^{F} is treated as constant. We replace the original infeasibility shaping term with

ℒinf​-​margin=1|ℐ|​∑k∈ℐ[EmaxF+log⁡(1+νk)−Eθ​(G,𝐲k)]+,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{inf\text{-}margin}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}|}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}}\left[E_{\max}^{F}+\log(1+\nu_{k})-E_{\theta}(G,\mathbf{y}_{k})\right]_{+},

where [a]+=max⁡(0,a)[a]_{+}=\max(0,a) and νk\nu_{k} is the normalized constraint violation. This term penalizes an infeasible candidate unless its energy lies at least log⁡(1+νk)\log(1+\nu_{k}) above the highest energy feasible candidate in the sampled candidate pool, thereby explicitly enforcing feasible–infeasible ordering within that pool.

We evaluate this alternative under the same Combinatorial Auctions protocol using EnerGNN with the linear head, which is the best performing EnerGNN variant for CA.

The stricter loss enforces the desired ordering but substantially reduces solution quality: the mean gap increases from 0.20% to 3.96%, exact recovery decreases from 67% to 4%, and the fraction of solutions within 1% of optimality decreases from 95% to 18%. Both variants return feasible solutions on every test instance.

This result clarifies the role of infeasibility supervision. The ranking and calibration terms are not intended to learn a global feasibility certificate, feasibility with respect to the encoded constraints is enforced by the inference MIP. Complete feasible–infeasible separation is therefore not required when those constraints are explicitly encoded, and in this experiment enforcing it substantially degrades optimization quality.

J.4 Readout Design Ablation

We evaluate how the choice of MIP-compatible readout affects solution quality and inference time. The proposed readouts combine pooled learned embeddings with compact structural summaries. We compare them with simpler embedding-only readouts and with variants that concatenate the complete binary decision vector 𝐲\mathbf{y} directly to the learned embedding pools. The latter reduces the need for structured summaries but produces an order-dependent, dimension-specific input.

For CA, removing the compact scalar summaries leaves performance essentially unchanged, while directly exposing the complete decision vector provides no improvement. For QKP, the structured readout is substantially more effective: the mean gap decreases from 0.81% to 0.31% and the fraction within 1% increases from 72% to 99%. Directly concatenating the full decision vector performs worse.

These results indicate that EnerGNN does not require a large collection of hand-crafted features. A practical readout should remain compact, permutation-invariant where possible, compatible with varying problem sizes, and exactly MIP-representable. Pooled learned embeddings can provide most of the representation, while compact structural summaries are useful when they capture meaningful consequences of the selected configuration.

Appendix K Baseline Implementation Details

All neural methods use the same bipartite GNN encoder architecture, with method-specific prediction or energy heads. We describe these heads, training objectives, and inference procedures below.

Predict+Search.

Predict+Search applies a single linear layer to each variable embedding, followed by a sigmoid, to predict its probability pjp_{j} of taking value one. The model is trained using binary cross entropy supervision on the variable assignments of positive candidate solutions. At inference, we rank variables by confidence |pj−0.5||p_{j}-0.5| and fix the most confident 85% for QKP and 80% for CA to their predicted values 𝟏[pj≥0.5]\mathbf{1}[p_{j}\geq 0.5]. For CART, we instead use a two-sided confidence band, where facility variables with pj≥0.6p_{j}\geq 0.6 are fixed to one, those with pj≤0.4p_{j}\leq 0.4 are fixed to zero, and the remaining facility variables are left free. We then solve the reduced MIP.

Linear+MIP.

Linear+MIP applies a single linear layer to each variable embedding to produce a scalar score sjs_{j}. These scores define an additive objective s⁡(y)=∑jsj​yjs(y)=\sum_{j}s_{j}y_{j}, which is maximized under the original hard constraints. We evaluate two training variants with the same architecture: (i) binary cross entropy supervision on variable assignments, using σ⁡(sj)\sigma(s_{j}) as the predicted probability, and (ii) contrastive supervision over candidate solutions, using the energy E⁡(y)=−s⁡(y)E(y)=-s(y). At inference, both variants optimize the learned linear objective over all decision variables using a MIP solver.

Neural Diving.

Our Neural Diving (Nair et al., 2020) baseline uses a two-layer variable-level MLP head, with one hidden layer of width dhd_{h}, a ReLU activation, and dropout, followed by a sigmoid, to predict an independent Bernoulli probability pjp_{j} for each binary decision variable. The model is trained with binary cross entropy supervision on the variable assignments of positive candidate solutions. At inference, we perform KK stochastic dives by sampling candidate assignments from these Bernoulli probabilities. For each dive, a confidence-selected subset of variables is fixed to the sampled assignment, and the reduced MIP is optimized over the remaining free variables. The final solution is the best feasible solution found across all dives. We use K=20K=20 dives for QKP, K=8K=8 for CART, and K=100K=100 for CA. The smaller dive budget for CART reflects the higher computational cost of solving its reduced MIPs. For QKP and CA, we fix the most confident 85% and 50% of variables, respectively. For CART, because the number of facility variables is small, we instead use the same two-sided confidence band as Predict+Search: variables with pj≥0.6p_{j}\geq 0.6 or pj≤0.4p_{j}\leq 0.4 are fixed to their sampled values, and the remaining variables are left free.

ConPaS.

Our controlled ConPaS-style (Huang et al., 2024) baseline applies a 3-layer variable-level MLP head, with 2 hidden layers of width 64 and ReLU activations, followed by a sigmoid, to predict independent Bernoulli probabilities pjp_{j} for the binary decision variables. It scores a candidate assignment by its factorized log probability,

s⁡(y)=∑jyj​log⁡pj+(1−yj)​log⁡(1−pj).s(y)=\sum_{j}y_{j}\log p_{j}+(1-y_{j})\log(1-p_{j}).

Training uses an InfoNCE contrastive loss over the candidate pool, encouraging positive solutions to receive higher scores than suboptimal feasible and infeasible candidates. At inference, the neural model is not embedded in the MIP. Instead, variables are ranked by pjp_{j}. Let X0X_{0} denote the k0k_{0} lowest probability variables and X1X_{1} the k1k_{1} highest probability variables. We solve the original MIP with the additional rank-neighbourhood constraint

∑j∈X0yj+∑j∈X1(1−yj)≤Δ,\sum_{j\in X_{0}}y_{j}+\sum_{j\in X_{1}}(1-y_{j})\leq\Delta,

which allows at most Δ\Delta disagreements with the predicted low/high probability sets while leaving all other variables unrestricted. Increasing Δ\Delta relaxes this rank-neighbourhood restriction by allowing more disagreements with the neural ranking. This can improve solution quality under constraint shift, where variables predicted to be unlikely may become necessary because of exogenous constraints, but it also enlarges the MIP search space. We therefore tune Δ\Delta per benchmark to balance solution quality and solve time. The rank-neighbourhood parameters are (k0,k1,Δ)=(55,20,5)(k_{0},k_{1},\Delta)=(55,20,5) for QKP, (8,2,1)(8,2,1) for CART, and (88,0,3)(88,0,3) for CA. For CA, we keep the paper-scaled choice k0=⌊n/2⌋k_{0}=\lfloor n/2\rfloor used by ConPaS. The original in-distribution ConPaS setting uses Δ=0\Delta=0. However, under our constraint shift setting, exogenous outage and force-on constraints can make a small number of low-ranked bids necessary. We therefore introduce a small slack of Δ=3\Delta=3. We also evaluated the stricter paper-style setting (88,0,0)(88,0,0), but it produced poor solution quality, with a mean gap of 6.23%6.23\%, despite being fast, with an average solve time of 0.050.05s compared with Gurobi’s 0.140.14s.

Broader Impact

This work develops learning-augmented optimization methods for constrained combinatorial decision-making. A potential positive impact is to make learned decision systems more reliable in settings where feasibility is essential, such as logistics, supply chain planning, manufacturing, and healthcare operations. Rather than producing decisions directly, EnerGNN learns an objective landscape that is optimized under explicit hard constraints. This may help decision-support tools adapt to changing demand, capacity, or operational requirements while preserving feasibility through the optimization layer. In personalized medicine supply chains, such methods could support the evaluation of strategic planning decisions under different patient demand and capacity scenarios. More broadly, the approach may be useful in domains where learned models must interact with exact algorithms to produce valid decisions. The method is not intended to replace domain expertise, clinical judgement, or human oversight in high-stakes settings. Exact constrained inference preserves feasibility with respect to the specified constraints, but it does not guarantee that the learned energy ranks all decisions correctly or that the specified objective captures all clinical, ethical, or operational priorities. If deployed without careful validation, a learned energy could favor suboptimal allocations or reinforce undesirable trade-offs.
